data.name: Honey Rose: Underdog Fighter Extraordinaire
data.detailed_description:
IMPORTANT NOTE: For all information regarding DLC and the "Pay-what-you-like" remuneration model, please read the information below!

What the game is about:

Honey Rose: UFE tells the story of Red, a young university student with dreams of making it big at the masked fighting tournament.
She looks up to Big Blue, the current champion, and aims to meet her idol in the ring! However, she has a history of poor class attendance, and has repeatedly failed her latest classes.
This year, she made a deal with her parents: she’d either graduate, or they’d change towns. Unfortunately, the masked fighting tournament also takes place for the first time in the very town Red lives in... making it her one and only chance to make her dream come true!

Thankfully, that’s where you come in!

With your guidance, she needs to balance her studies with her training so she can bring home both the champion's belt, and her graduation.

The game is a life-management simulation, presented as a visual novel, with beat'em-up elements.

In short: some reading, a little fighting... and lots of planning!


Features:

  • A visual novel based around choice and reactivity! See how events unfold based on your decisions... or lack of commitment!
  • A sizeable cast of characters to encounter in dynamic events, with individual subplots to pursue!
  • Fight for your dreams in the ring, or to get back your suit from dastardly thugs in the street!
  • Plan ahead to make the most of the 6 months you have left until graduation!
  • Bring home the champion's belt if you can, but make sure to ace your tests as well! Can you really do both?


Pricing

The game uses a "pay-what-you-liked" remuneration model.

"Pay-what-you-liked" is a system designed after "pay-what-you-want", except you choose to support the game *after* having played it for yourself, and determined its personal value based on your own experience. It is designed to offer each player the most choice possible in how, when and why when considering whether to support the game or not.

Since Steam doesn't support "pay-what-you-liked" or "pay-what-you-want" remuneration systems, the DLC acts as a stand-in to offer multiple suggested tiers of support.

IMPORTANT NOTE: buying DLC stands in for supporting the game at the value of the suggested tier. It will NOT enhance or change your ingame experience, you will not be getting additional content other players can't access, as the aim for this system is for the game to be the same for everyone: ie, its most complete state right off the bat! That also means the game is NOT F2P/P2W: there is NO in-game economy that allows you to pay for additional content. The game is fully available for free from the minute you start playing it!

data.short_description: One student, two lives and six months to go. This year, Red must meet her idol Big Blue in the ring and make it to the top of the masked fighting tournament. Her dream will come true... as long as she also graduates!

reviews.review:
Honey Rose: Underdog Fighter Extraordinaire is a really unusual game, and I think that is the main reason I enjoyed it. I am looking after Red, a university student who wants to become a masked fighting champion while also trying to graduate. I only have six months to get everything done, so I have to decide how I spend my time instead of being able to train, study and socialise whenever I want. Most of the game is planning and reading, with the actual fighting coming in at important moments. It is a strange combination, but the different parts fit together better than I expected.

The planning is easily my favourite part. I have to balance Red's studies with her training, and wasting too much time in one area can cause problems somewhere else. I also have to deal with different events and characters, so there is more going on than simply increasing a few stats until the final tournament arrives. I like having to think ahead because it gives my choices some weight. The six month limit also means I cannot just take my time and eventually do everything. I have to decide what actually matters to me during that particular run.

The visual novel side is also much better than I expected from a game that is partly about fighting. There is a proper cast of characters and individual subplots, and the events can change depending on what I choose to do or ignore. Red's situation gives the story a simple goal that I can understand straight away. She wants to meet Big Blue, her idol and the current champion, but she also has to prove that she can actually graduate. I like that these two goals are constantly competing with each other instead of the story just telling me that everything will work out.

The fighting is where I have the most mixed feelings. I like that I actually have to control Red during the matches instead of just watching the results of my training. There are proper one on one fights in the tournament, as well as fights outside the ring, including situations where Red has to deal with groups of enemies. The combat gives me a nice break from all the reading and planning, but it is also fairly basic compared with a game that is built entirely around fighting. For me, that is fine because the combat is supporting the life management side rather than trying to replace it.

I do think the game can become repetitive when I start replaying it. The whole point is to make different decisions and see how things turn out, but getting to those different outcomes means going through some of the same planning and story sections again. That is where I start noticing the limitations. The game has a good amount of character content for such a small project, but it does not have the huge amount of variety that I would expect from a much larger life simulator. The six month structure works well, but it also means I am repeating a familiar routine when I want to try another approach.

One thing I really appreciate is that the complete game is available without paying for the actual content. The developer uses a pay what you liked system, where the different DLC purchases are basically ways to support the game rather than unlocking extra gameplay. That makes a big difference to me because I can play the whole thing first and decide whether I want to support it afterwards. There are also 37 achievements, which gives me another reason to experiment with different outcomes instead of stopping after I finish one successful run.

Overall, Honey Rose is one of those games where I like the idea almost as much as the actual game. Balancing university, training and Red's dream of becoming a champion gives me something to think about every time I make a decision, and the visual novel sections have enough personality to keep me interested. The fighting is fun but not deep enough to carry the game by itself, and replaying the same early sections can get tiring when I am chasing different outcomes. Still, I think the unusual combination works, and the fact that I get the complete game without having to pay for it makes the rougher parts much easier to accept. It is not a perfect fighting game or life simulator, but as a small and genuinely different game, I think it deserves a fair bit of credit.

Rating: 7.7/10
